bib.title: The Golem of Prague (Chapter 1 of Statistical Rethinking)

read.skipped: endnotes (superscript markers 1-34) are not in the PDF text; year not printed in the chapter (text mentions 2015 as a recent date)

question: Why should statistical inference be rethought as building and comparing models rather than choosing pre-made tests to falsify null hypotheses?
contributions: Frames statistical models as golems: powerful, obedient, without wisdom
Argues deductive falsification fails because hypotheses are not models and measurement is error-prone
Introduces three tools: Bayesian data analysis, multilevel models, information criteria
Outlines the book in four parts

results.claim: Hypotheses, process models and statistical models relate many-to-many, so rejecting or failing to reject a null model cannot strictly falsify or confirm a hypothesis.
results.quote: Hypotheses do not imply unique models, and models do not imply unique hypotheses.

results.claim: Falsification is consensual, not logical, because of measurement error and continuous hypotheses.
results.quote: But falsification is always consensual, not logical.

results.claim: Bayesian inference is counting the ways things can happen under assumptions; probability is a calculus of plausibility, not a belief system.
results.quote: Bayesian inference is no more than counting the numbers of ways things can happen, according to our assumptions.

results.claim: Frequentist inference grounds uncertainty in imagined resampling; Bayesian treats randomness as a property of information, so it works when measurement is deterministic (Saturn example).
results.quote: Bayesian golems treat “randomness” as a property of information, not of the world.

results.claim: Multilevel regression should be the default form of regression.
results.quote: multilevel regression deserves to be the default form of regression.

results.claim: Information criteria estimate predictive accuracy rather than fit, guarding against overfitting and allowing comparison of several non-null models.
results.quote: fitting is easy; prediction is hard.

results.claim: Maximum-entropy (exponential family) distributions mean a fitted regression cannot identify the underlying process, yet remain useful.
results.quote: one can no more infer evolutionary process from a power law than one can infer developmental process from the fact that height is normally distributed.

results.claim: Scientists commonly misread p-values and confidence intervals as Bayesian posterior and credible intervals; the reverse mistake is rare, a pedagogical argument for Bayes.
results.quote: interpreting ordinary p-values as Bayesian posterior probabilities and non-Bayesian confidence intervals as Bayesian ones

limits: Conceptual argument with no data; the author concedes Bayesian methods remain computationally expensive and approximations will stay important (p13).
Information criteria are young with no consensus on best metric (p16).
Bayesian results are not claimed more correct, only closer to scientists' intuitions (p13).
Mentions ivory-billed woodpecker status 'by 2015', so dated.
practices: Work through the computational nuts and bolts of each model rather than pushing buttons until wise enough (p4).
Explicitly compare predictions of more than one process model, and look for a description of the evidence under which the processes differ (p7).
Prefer building and comparing multiple non-null models over testing a single null hypothesis (p16).
Use multilevel models for repeat sampling, imbalanced sampling, studying variation, and avoiding pre-averaging (p14).
Do not judge models by fit alone; use information criteria for predictive accuracy (p15-16).
Papers not using multilevel models should justify not doing so (p14).

a model in which a parameter is regarded as a placeholder for a missing model, giving multiple levels of uncertainty; also hierarchical, random effects, varying effects, mixed effects
